summary: This informational document establishes a common understanding of baseline scenarios for evaluating different information-centric networking (ICN) approaches, so they can be tested and compared against each other.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes common situations for testing information-centric networking designs. Researchers can use the same kinds of scenarios to compare different approaches more fairly.

subtitle: Baseline scenarios for comparing information-centric networking approaches.

tldr.problem: Different information-centric networking proposals have been evaluated with different scenarios, making results difficult to compare fairly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys prior research and describes nine scenario categories plus cross-cutting concerns for evaluation.
tldr.outcome: This IRTF Informational document offers a research framework, not a standard or a required test plan; evaluation methods and metrics are covered separately.

today: RFC 7476 is an Informational document from the IRTF published in March 2015. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC says evaluation methodology and metrics are handled separately.

sections.title: Why Baseline Scenarios Matter
sections.content:
Information-centric networking (ICN) shifts attention from a communicating host to named information. It can use in-network storage and support communication when connectivity is intermittent.

Several ICN architectures were under development, and researchers often chose different evaluation setups. This RFC surveys published work to identify scenarios that can help compare approaches; it does not define a standard or evaluation methodology.
sections.plainLanguage: ICN research includes different designs, and different tests can make comparisons difficult. This RFC collects scenarios that researchers can use as common starting points.

sections.title: Nine Scenario Categories
sections.content:
The RFC describes social networking, real-time communication, mobile networking, infrastructure sharing, content dissemination, vehicular networking, delay- and disruption-tolerance, the Internet of Things, and smart cities.

Each scenario highlights different questions. Examples include caching and multicast for shared content, service continuity during mobility, and delivery when networks are disconnected. The categories can overlap rather than forming rigid boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The scenarios cover social services, calls, mobile devices, shared resources, content delivery, vehicles, disruptions, connected objects, and cities. Each puts different network abilities under test.

sections.title: Issues Shared Across Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC highlights multiply connected nodes and their economic implications, energy efficiency, and operation across different network technologies. A device may use several access networks, while those networks can have different owners and policies.

ICN evaluation should also consider energy used by devices and networks, including the costs of name processing and caching. Designs need to operate with existing network technologies and across boundaries between different network paradigms.
sections.plainLanguage: Several questions apply to many scenarios: how devices use multiple networks, how much energy they need, and how different network technologies work together.

sections.title: What Evaluations Should Measure
sections.content:
The RFC identifies evaluation aspects including network efficiency, reduced complexity, scalability, reliability, mobility, multicast and caching, real-time communication, energy consumption, delay and disruption tolerance, information security and trust, persistence, availability, provenance, and location independence.

It refers to separate work for evaluation methodology and metric definitions. It emphasizes that results should account for technical behavior and, where relevant, operational and economic trade-offs.
sections.plainLanguage: Comparisons should measure the properties that matter to each scenario, such as delay, reliability, energy, or scalability. The method for running evaluations is described in a separate document.

sections.title: Scope and Research Status
sections.content:
RFC 7476 reflects the consensus of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group after a survey of peer-reviewed literature. It is an Informational research document and does not require researchers to follow its scenarios.

The summary encourages evaluation across different application areas and notes that further research is needed on technical, operational, economic, and resource trade-offs.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a shared research reference, not a rule. Researchers can use its scenarios while continuing to develop other tests and approaches.
